Options¶

Back to Least Squares

struct reg::OLSOptions {
  double alpha = 0.05;
  bool add_intercept = true;
  bool drop_missing = true;
  double rcond = 1e-12;
  std::string response_name = "y";
  std::vector<std::string> predictor_names{};
  reg::OLSCovarianceType covariance = reg::OLSCovarianceType::Nonrobust;
};

Option

Effect

Default

alpha

the intervals have coverage 1 − alpha; must lie strictly between 0 and 1

0.05

add_intercept

add a column of ones in front of the predictors

true

drop_missing

drop rows with a non-finite value; false makes them an error (Missing data)

true

weights

precision weights for weighted least squares (Case weights)

none

rcond

relative cutoff below which a direction of the design counts as rank deficient; must be positive (Collinear predictors)

1e-12

response_name, predictor_names

labels used by the summary and coefficient_names (Shapes and inputs)

"y", none

covariance

the covariance estimator; Nonrobust is the only one, s² (X′X)⁻¹

Nonrobust

This page shows alpha, add_intercept and covariance.

The confidence level¶

alpha fixes the critical multiplier of the intervals and changes nothing else: the coefficients, standard errors, t values and p-values are the same at every level. A smaller alpha (a higher confidence level) gives wider intervals, and each interval contains the narrower ones.

#include <pluss/ma.h>
#include <pluss/tils/aux/output.h>

namespace reg = pluss::subsp::stats::regression;
using namespace pluss::tils;

int main() {
  OutputEngine out;
  out.print_defaults(PrintOptions{}.fixed(4));
  const auto x = pluss::make_series(std::vector<double>{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8}, {8}, as_f64());
  const auto y = pluss::make_series(std::vector<double>{2.1, 3.9, 6.2, 7.8, 10.1, 12.2, 13.8, 16.1}, {8}, as_f64());
  out.writeln(" alpha  confidence   slope interval            std error   p value of the slope");
  for (double alpha : {0.50, 0.10, 0.05, 0.01, 0.001}) {
    reg::OLSOptions options;
    options.alpha = alpha;
    const auto fit = reg::ols_fit(y, x, options);
    const auto ci = fit.conf_int.host<double>().array().data;
    out.writeln(alpha, " ", 1.0 - alpha, "   [", ci[2], ",", ci[3], "]", fit.std_errors.pull<double>()[1], fit.p_values.pull<double>()[1], " alpha stored:", fit.alpha);
  }
}

Output

 alpha  confidence   slope interval            std error   p value of the slope
0.5000   0.5000    [ 1.9777 , 2.0176 ] 0.0278 0.0000  alpha stored: 0.5000
0.1000   0.9000    [ 1.9436 , 2.0516 ] 0.0278 0.0000  alpha stored: 0.1000
0.0500   0.9500    [ 1.9296 , 2.0656 ] 0.0278 0.0000  alpha stored: 0.0500
0.0100   0.9900    [ 1.8946 , 2.1007 ] 0.0278 0.0000  alpha stored: 0.0100
0.0010   0.9990    [ 1.8320 , 2.1633 ] 0.0278 0.0000  alpha stored: 0.0010

The standard error and the p-value are the same in every row: alpha enters only through the multiplier. The interval grows from [1.9777, 2.0176] at 50% to [1.8320, 2.1633] at 99.9%, each containing the one before it, and the result stores the alpha it used.

With and without an intercept¶

add_intercept = false forces the line through the origin. The const coefficient disappears, k_params drops by one, df_model equals the rank, and the totals are taken about zero (Every number in the result). Fitting through the origin is right when the response is known to be zero at zero predictors; it is wrong, and visibly so in the residuals, when it is not. The program fits data with a real offset both ways.

#include <pluss/ma.h>
#include <pluss/tils/aux/output.h>

namespace reg = pluss::subsp::stats::regression;
using namespace pluss::tils;

int main() {
  OutputEngine out;
  out.print_defaults(PrintOptions{}.fixed(4));
  const auto x = pluss::make_series(std::vector<double>{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8}, {8}, as_f64());
  const auto offset = pluss::make_series(std::vector<double>{5.1, 6.9, 9.2, 10.8, 13.1, 15.2, 16.8, 19.1}, {8}, as_f64());  // 3 + 2x
  const auto proportional = pluss::make_series(std::vector<double>{2.1, 3.9, 6.2, 7.8, 10.1, 12.2, 13.8, 16.1}, {8}, as_f64());  // 2x

  reg::OLSOptions origin;
  origin.add_intercept = false;
  for (int pass = 0; pass < 2; ++pass) {
    const auto &y = pass == 0 ? offset : proportional;
    const auto with = reg::ols_fit(y, x);
    const auto without = reg::ols_fit(y, x, origin);
    out.writeln(pass == 0 ? "response 3 + 2x:" : "response 2x    :", "with intercept", with.coefficients.pull<double>(), " rmse", with.rmse);
    out.writeln("                through origin", without.coefficients.pull<double>(), " rmse", without.rmse, " names", without.coefficient_names);
    out.writeln("                residual mean (zero when an intercept is fitted):", with.residuals.mean().item<double>(), "vs", without.residuals.mean().item<double>());
  }
}

Output

response 3 + 2x: with intercept [3.0357, 1.9976]  rmse 0.1802
                through origin [2.5333]  rmse 1.4820  names [x1]
                residual mean (zero when an intercept is fitted): -0.0000 vs 0.6250
response 2x    : with intercept [0.0357, 1.9976]  rmse 0.1802
                through origin [2.0039]  rmse 0.1677  names [x1]
                residual mean (zero when an intercept is fitted): -0.0000 vs 0.0074

For the response 3 + 2x, the free intercept recovers 3.0357 and 1.9976, while the line forced through the origin has slope 2.5333, a root mean square error of 1.48 against 0.18, and residuals that average 0.625 instead of zero: a visible bias. For the response 2x, the through-origin fit is sound (slope 2.0039, residual mean 0.0074) and its root mean square error, 0.1677, is slightly below 0.1802 because it estimates one parameter fewer. The residuals average exactly zero only when an intercept is fitted.

The covariance estimator¶

OLSCovarianceType currently has one member, Nonrobust, the classical estimate s² (X′X)⁻¹ that assumes errors with constant variance. The result records the choice in covariance_type, and the summary prints it. For errors whose variance changes with a predictor, see the quantile chapter, whose Robust covariance does not assume that.

#include <pluss/ma.h>
#include <pluss/tils/aux/output.h>

namespace reg = pluss::subsp::stats::regression;
using namespace pluss::tils;

int main() {
  OutputEngine out;
  const auto x = pluss::make_series(std::vector<double>{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8}, {8}, as_f64());
  const auto y = pluss::make_series(std::vector<double>{2.1, 3.9, 6.2, 7.8, 10.1, 12.2, 13.8, 16.1}, {8}, as_f64());
  reg::OLSOptions options;
  options.covariance = reg::OLSCovarianceType::Nonrobust;
  const auto fit = reg::ols_fit(y, x, options);
  out.writeln("covariance_type is Nonrobust:", fit.covariance_type == reg::OLSCovarianceType::Nonrobust ? "yes" : "no");
  out.writeln("it is s2 (X'X)^-1, so the standard errors scale with sqrt(mse): mse", fit.mse, " rmse", fit.rmse);
}

Output

covariance_type is Nonrobust: yes
it is s2 (X'X)^-1, so the standard errors scale with sqrt(mse): mse 0.03246031746031756  rmse 0.18016747059421565

The result records the estimator; the standard errors are the square roots of the diagonal of s²(X′X)⁻¹, scaled by the residual standard deviation, 0.1802 here.
